data.text/html:
The Cox proportional hazards model, explained interactively

An explorable companion to TileStats' video "The Cox proportional hazards model explained". Cox regression answers one question: how much does a variable multiply your risk of dying right now? It never says when anyone dies. It only compares people who are still alive at the same moment.

data.text/markdown:
Roadmap (same order as the video).
  1. From the Kaplan–Meier curve to the hazard ||(h(t)||) and the cumulative hazard ||(H(t)||)
  2. Two groups, one hazard ratio: ||(h_A(t) = h_0(t)\,e^{\beta}||)
  3. How Cox actually fits ||(\beta||): the partial likelihood, plus the R-style output (HR, CI, p-value, ||(1/\text{HR}||))
  4. Beyond the log-rank test: adjusting for age
  5. Checking the proportional hazards assumption with a log-minus-log plot
Then a sandbox (a live survival race), a quiz and a recap. Color language used everywhere: ■ group A (old treatment, ||(x=1||)) · ■ group B (new treatment, the baseline, ||(x=0||)) · ■ the key quantity (||(\beta||), the hazard ratio, the fitted curve) · ■ censored / not at risk A separate notebook (survival_analysis.py) covers Kaplan–Meier basics; here we focus on Cox.

1 · From the Kaplan–Meier curve to the hazard

The video starts with six subjects. One dies after 1 year (||(S = 5/6 \approx 0.83||)), the next after 6 years (||(S=4/6\approx0.67||)), and so on. The hazard is the risk of dying in the next small time step, given you survived until ||(t||): ||[h(t) = \lim_{\Delta t\to 0}\frac{P(t \le T < t+\Delta t \mid T \ge t)}{\Delta t} \;=\; -\frac{S'(t)}{S(t)}||]With yearly steps, as in the video, we estimate it per interval as ||(\hat h = \dfrac{\text{deaths}}{\text{at risk}\times\text{interval length}}||). Between year 1 and year 6, one of five people died over five years, so ||(\hat h = 1/(5\cdot5)=0.04||) per year. The cumulative hazard adds up hazard × time: ||(H(t)=\int_0^t h(u)\,du||). (The video's description corrects an error at 4:12: you must multiply each hazard by its interval length, giving 0.1667, 0.3667, 0.6167, 1.2833, 2.2833.) Drag a subject's end marker left/right to change when they die. Click a marker to toggle death (●) ↔ censored (○).

data.text/markdown:
2 · Two groups and the hazard ratio

Now 12 subjects: group A (old treatment) and group B (new treatment). B is the baseline (||(x=0||)), A has ||(x=1||). The video's rough intuition: take the log of each group's estimated hazards, and fit two straight lines that are forced to have the same slope. Then the lines differ only by a vertical shift ||(\beta||): ||[\log h_A(t) = \underbrace{a + b\,t}_{\log h_0(t)} + \beta\cdot 1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad h_A(t) = h_0(t)\,e^{\beta}||]so ||(e^{\beta}||) is the hazard ratio (HR): at every time point, A's hazard is ||(e^\beta||) times B's. That is the whole Cox model: ||(\;h(t\mid x) = h_0(t)\,e^{\beta x}||). Parallel on the log scale = proportional on the raw scale. (The real Cox fit doesn't do this regression; it uses the partial likelihood of section 3. The video's simplified fit gives β≈1.1 and the true Cox fit gives 1.25. Our made-up data lands in a similar spot.)

data.text/markdown:
3 · How Cox really fits β: the partial likelihood

The video skips this ("it's quite complicated"), but the idea is a simple game. At every death, ask: of everyone still at risk, why this person? Under ||(h_i(t)=h_0(t)e^{\beta x_i}||), the probability that the death hit subject ||(i||) is ||[P(i \mid \text{one death at } t) = \frac{h_0(t)\,e^{\beta x_i}}{\sum_{j\in R(t)} h_0(t)\,e^{\beta x_j}} = \frac{e^{\beta x_i}}{\sum_{j\in R(t)} e^{\beta x_j}}||]The baseline hazard ||(h_0(t)||) cancels. That's why Cox never needs to know its shape. Multiply these probabilities over all deaths to get the partial likelihood ||(L(\beta)||); the ||(\hat\beta||) that maximises it is the Cox estimate. Step through the deaths. Bars are subjects (still at risk = solid, gone = faded). The number at the right of each at-risk bar is that subject's chance of being "the one" under your β.

The maximum balances both.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eRead the output like the video: the CI for HR is wide and includes \u003cstrong\u003e1\u003c/strong\u003e, and p &gt; 0.05. With 12 people, we can't reject \"no difference\". \u003ccode\u003eexp(-coef)\u003c/code\u003e is the HR with A as baseline.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
4 · Why not just a log-rank test? Adding age

To compare two groups, the log-rank test is enough (above, it's literally Cox's score test). Cox's advantage is that it's a regression: add more variables and each gets its own hazard ratio, controlling for the others. ||[h(t\mid x, \text{age}) = h_0(t)\,\exp(\beta_1 x + \beta_2\,\text{age})||]The video's example: ||(\hat\beta_2 = 0.095 \Rightarrow e^{0.095}\approx 1.10||). Each extra year of age raises the hazard by ~10%, holding group fixed. Below we simulate a bigger trial where group A also tends to be older. Watch what happens to the group HR when we forget to adjust for age.

data.text/html: 600 subjects, 373 deaths. Orange dashed line = true HR. Mean age: A 68.5, B 61.1.

<marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTry this\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eSet \u003cstrong\u003etrue β₁ = 0\u003c/strong\u003e (treatment does nothing) and age gap = 15. The unadjusted model \"finds\" a strong treatment effect that is pure \u003cstrong\u003econfounding by age\u003c/strong\u003e. The adjusted model recovers HR ≈ 1.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eSet the age gap to 0. Both models now agree on the group HR, because adjusting doesn't matter when the groups are balanced.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eThe video's likelihood-ratio test compares the two nested models: a big χ² means adding age improves the fit.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eAn HR per year of 1.10 compounds: 10 years older ⇒ \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(1.1^{10}\\approx e^{0.95}\\approx 2.6\\times||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e the hazard.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
5 · Checking the proportional hazards assumption

Cox assumes the HR is constant over time. If the Kaplan–Meier curves cross, that's hard to believe: A is riskier early, B is riskier later. The video's check is the log-minus-log plot. Since ||(S(t)=e^{-H(t)}||) and under PH ||(H_A(t)=e^\beta H_0(t)||): ||[\log\!\big(-\log S_A(t)\big) = \beta + \log\!\big(-\log S_B(t)\big)||]so plotted against ||(\log t||), the two curves should be parallel, a constant vertical distance ||(\beta||) apart.

<marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTry this\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eProportional\u003c/strong\u003e: the log-minus-log curves are parallel, the gap is ≈ log 2, and every \"implied HR\" is ≈ 2, matching Cox.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eCrossing hazards\u003c/strong\u003e: the KM curves cross and the log-minus-log curves \u003cstrong\u003ecross\u003c/strong\u003e too. Cox still prints a single HR, but it's an average of \"A worse early\" and \"B worse late\", and describes neither period.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eEffect wears off\u003c/strong\u003e: the curves \u003cem\u003econverge\u003c/em\u003e. The one-number HR understates the early benefit of B and overstates the late one. (Fixes: stratify, time-varying coefficients, or report HRs per period.)\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"warn"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
Sandbox · The survival race

Two groups of people live through time. At each tick, everyone still alive in group B dies with probability ||(h_0(t)\,\Delta t||); in group A with ||(h_0(t)\,e^{\beta}\,\Delta t||). The baseline ||(h_0(t)||) is a Weibull hazard whose shape you choose (shape < 1: risk falls over time; = 1: constant; > 1: risk rises). Press ▶ race. When the race ends at ||(t=20||) (or when you pause), the results go to Python, which fits a Cox model. Can Cox recover your β, whatever the baseline shape?
